content.thinking:
I'll write a fresh koala.ts file from scratch. I'm picturing a pixel-art koala gripping a vertical eucalyptus log mounted on a wooden base stand, like a viewing perch.

Thinking through the pose: should the koala's belly press against the trunk with its back to the viewer, or should it be angled so its face is visible? I'll go with a slightly turned clinging pose so the face reads clearly while its limbs wrap around the bark, which also gives it branches with leaf clusters for extra detail.

Trying to settle the composition: trunk vertical behind the koala at z=-0.22, with the koala sitting upright facing forward, back near the trunk. I'm weighing whether to add a horizontal perch branch jutting forward for the legs and a diagonal branch for the arms to grip, but it's getting complex, so I want to simplify into a clean, readable arrangement with just a trunk and maybe one or two supporting branches.

Let me reconsider the whole pose: maybe simpler to have the branch run along X instead, with the koala sitting astride it rump-up, legs dangling forward, perhaps gripping a lower support branch with its feet rather than wrapping the same branch awkwardly.

I'll go with the hugging pose instead—body facing forward so arms wrap around the trunk in front, with the trunk positioned slightly off-center and the arm tips reaching to wrap its front face. That keeps the face readable from camera while making the cling/hug gesture physically believable.

Actually, a simpler symmetrical design might work better and reduce risk: a forward-facing koala sitting upright in the fork of a Y-shaped branch stand, with a trunk behind and two branches forking up into a V. Hands grip each branch arm while feet grip the trunk-fork below, giving a clear, symmetric, face-forward look.

Maybe instead koala hugs a branch running front-to-back, belly draped over it with arms and legs wrapped around the sides, head lifted up facing forward over the branch — more like the classic koala-hugging-a-log pose than sitting upright on a perch.

I'll put the trunk on the right side with the koala hugging it on the left, face toward the camera, and nudge the positions so the whole composition stays roughly centered. I also want the koala's torso leaning back slightly from the trunk with arms reaching to it, which reads as a more natural clinging pose, and I'm starting to rough out proportions like seated height for the model.

Now I'm roughing out specific coordinates: hips, shoulders, head, and feet positions for the climbing koala, with the trunk extending up to about 1.7m topped by branches and leaves, giving a total height near 1.8m.

I'm adding a small stub branch jutting out from the trunk for the koala's rump to rest on, then setting precise trunk dimensions—center position, tapering radius, height, and a slight curved lean—along with planning the bark texture in pale gray tones.

I'm working out the koala's orientation: body facing toward the trunk, with the head turned to face sideways, and tracing through the rotation math to figure out which direction counts as its left versus right side.

Maybe a diagonal leaning branch would let the koala's face sit above the log while hugging it, but that feels overcomplicated. I'll just accept the rig-side naming as an internal labeling detail rather than a strict visual rule.

Actually, a cleaner solution is to make the whole pose symmetric: koala sitting upright, facing front, gripping a Y-shaped fork with both arms mirrored up the two branches — fully readable, rig-valid, and simple.

I'm overanalyzing the pose, so I'll just commit to a simpler symmetric design: a stepped octagonal wooden base, a vertical trunk post, with the koala sitting upright and gripping the forked branches above while feet brace lower down.

I'm working out the koala's shoulders, head, and arm positions, then calculating where its hands should grip the V-shaped branches so the pose looks natural, adjusting the branch width since the initial spread put the hands too close to the shoulders.

Thinking it through further, I'm weighing a vertically hugging pose against a front-facing one where the koala's arms reach up to grip branches on either side, like clinging to monkey bars—this reads as cute and symmetric with the head and ears nestled between the arms. I'm also considering an alternative where the koala grips a single horizontal branch with both hands in front of its body instead.

Settling on the final design: a stand with a base disc and vertical trunk behind, forking into a Y shape higher up, with a seat branch extending forward where the koala sits, leaning back against the trunk.

Now I'm working out the koala's grip and posture details -- arms raised to hold the two fork branches with clawed hands, feet planted on the seat branch with curling toes, and legs angled from hips to knees to complete a natural perched pose.

Now I'm working out stylized proportions for the head, ears, nose, and eyes, plus the pear-shaped torso with a lighter belly. I'm also settling on a cool grey fur palette with a cream belly, white fluffy ear interiors, and a dark nose with a highlight.

Setting the texel scale for the koala's voxel-pixel look, then planning the geometry approach: lofted/swept body sections along a spine chain combined with blocky boxes for the head (cranium, cheeks, muzzle) stacked ziggurat-style to get a rounded-pixel aesthetic similar to the capybara reference.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton: hip root branching into a spine chain up through chest, neck, head, and jaw, with hinge joints for the ears. For the limbs I'm planning shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand chains, and thinking through whether to give the koala hands separated digits — palm box plus finger rods plus an opposable thumb pair to match koala anatomy.

For the fingers gripping the branch, I'm deciding to curl each digit with a simple two-joint chain built from a short curve with two spans, so each finger bends around the branch without needing a tip joint. With five fingers per hand across two hands plus toes on each foot, that's roughly twenty small digit chains at two joints apiece, adding about forty joints total while staying within budget.

Now I'm working out how the hand actually wraps around the branch geometrically: I'll compute a circular path around the branch's axis, offset by the combined radius of branch and finger, sweeping through an angle to simulate gripping. I'm writing a helper function that takes the branch center, axis direction, a starting perpendicular direction, radius, sweep angle, and advance along the axis, then returns points along that spiral-like curve so each finger naturally follows the branch's curvature as it closes around it.

Computing that grip point puts the hand behind the shoulder in z, which fits a koala reaching back around the branch, though I'm now worried about the torso depth clipping into the trunk — I should adjust the trunk's z-position and radius so the koala's back surface doesn't overlap it.

Checking the gripshoulder distance against arm length confirms it fits, then I'm working out a seat branch extending forward from the trunk, and adjusting the stand's base disc position and radius so it centers under the trunk and covers the footprint properly.

Now I'm thinking about adding a diagonal support post from the base up to the seat's front tip, styled with rope-lashing rings in tan at the joints for detail. For the leaves, I'm planning eucalyptus-style sickle-shaped blue-green foliage using pixel-art leaf textures on cards.

Leaf cards need 8x16 pixel textures sized at double-sided frames clustered at branch tips plus along twigs, with smaller round juvenile leaves scattered nearby, keeping texel scale consistent with the koala's pixel density. I'm also planning thin twig rods with leaves oriented outward and small brown gum nut pods as additional details.

For the koala itself, I'm skipping a held leaf and giving it sleepy half-closed eyes instead, using small textured pixel planes for the beady eyes and a highlighted nose block. For the trunk, I'm painting a cream-gray eucalyptus bark base with orange, pink, and olive patches plus vertical streaks, using noise-based procedural painting to create peeling bark texture and a darker rough stocking pattern at the base.

Now I'm setting up color ramps: a bark ramp spanning dark brown to pale tan plus accent patch colors, a darker wood ramp for the base stand, and a cool gray-blue fur ramp for the koala with dithered shading driven by noise and per-cell randomness.

For the belly, I want a separate cream-colored patch within a defined chest region using position-based conditions, since koalas have a pale cream underside—wrapping this into a FUR_BODY paint that includes the belly while arms and other parts use a plain FUR paint without it.

I'm also adding a mottled pale rump patch on the lower back, plus facial details: a large black nose block, lighter muzzle paint, cream cheeks/chin, and big round ears built as extruded discs with grey outer fur, a fluffy cream inner disc, and small cream tufts along the edge to mimic a koala's characteristic ear fluff.

Positioning the ear planes angled slightly outward, then designing tiny pixel-art eyes as a 4x4 texture with a highlight pixel, planning to decal them onto the flat front face of the head box near the top.

Since the head is built from stepped boxes, I need a fixed reference point for placement—defining a head-center constant around (0, 1.04, 0.04) and a helper function to compute offsets from it so all head features (eyes, nose, face shape) align consistently in world space.

Now I'm laying out the skull shape: a broad rounded cranium, a slightly narrower crown layer on top, wide cheek layers for that koala fluffiness, and a protruding rounded muzzle box for the big nose, each positioned with careful z-depth offsets so the face reads as flat-fronted but still three-dimensional.

I'm positioning the nose, eyes, lower jaw, and mouth line relative to the cranium's front plane, nudging the eye depth slightly forward so they sit just proud of the face surface, and setting up the jaw as a separate hinge-aligned box for the lower lip and mouth interior.

Now I'm adding fluffy cheek tufts as small stepped cream triangular extrusions pointing outward from each cheek, sizing the big round ears and placing them high on the sides, and deciding to skip a brow ridge since koalas don't really have one. I'm also setting up a short neck joint connecting the head down to the shoulders before moving into the body's spine sweep starting from the hips.

Writing body section code...

Working through the vertical stacking: hips starting around 0.68 with the round cap extending down to roughly 0.5, torso widening to shoulders near 0.9, and head centered around 1.06 so the ears reach up to about 1.3. I'm mapping out body proportions from rump to head.

Now I'm planning the skeleton joint hierarchy, starting with the hips as root, then building a spine chain through a few intermediate points up toward the chest, matching the naming pattern used for the capybara rig where joint names correspond to segments along the curve.

I'm then adding a short neck chain continuing from the spine tip to the top of the neck, with a head joint oriented forward, before setting up the body sweep using a catmull curve through the full set of points, mirroring the capybara's bone list structure of hips, spine, and neck chains.

Skipping the tail for now. For the legs, I'm working out the joint positions for hips, knees, and ankles so the koala sits naturally with feet gripping the branch, figuring out how the toes should curve around the branch's surface.

Placing five toes per foot spread along the branch axis with small gripping arcs, and sketching the sole pad as a small box pressed against the branch side with the ankle positioned just above it.

Each toe gets sharp pale claw tips curving along the gripping path to mimic koala claws, and I'm working out how the arms and hands wrap around the V-shaped branches by sweeping fingers around the branch's cylindrical radius at the grip point.

Working out the finger and thumb sweep angles and offsets along the branch axis, spacing the three fingers and two thumbs on opposite sides of the palm so they wrap realistically around the branch.

All non-root parts need joints, so I'm giving the stand base its own joint attached under the hips root, keeping hips as the single root joint rather than introducing a separate stand root. Now I'm working out how the arm chain terminates at the wrist for the gripping hand.

Naming the arm joints as shoulder, elbow, and hand gives three points with two spans, with hand serving as the tip oriented along the path's end tangent, computed via the limb helper to get root, elbow, wrist positions. For the digits, I'm planning finger chains parented to that hand tip joint, using unique two-segment name arrays per finger to satisfy the naming constraints.

That's 20 digits total with 40 joints plus 20 claw spikes, using 6-sided sweeps with sparse rings. For accuracy I'm simplifying real koala anatomy: hands get 3 fingers plus 2 opposable thumbs, feet get 4 toes plus one clawless big toe. Now I'm moving to the eucalyptus trunk, sweeping it along a catmull path rising from the base.

Working out bark strip placement on the trunk surface...

Then I'm thinking through the foliage: eucalyptus leaves as hanging lanceolate cards along the twigs, using drooping flow vectors and leaning angles to get that sickle-shaped downward hang.

Better to set flow toward the camera so face normals point outward, keeping lean and bend at zero while using spin for rotational variety instead. I'll skip the cross setting and add slight spin variation, then move to leaf texture with a pixelArt style.

I'm designing a small sickle-shaped leaf sprite with a dark outline, muted green body, and lighter highlight/midrib tones, plus a bluish and greener variant along with a tiny round juvenile leaf texture. I'm planning leaf counts per branch cluster so the foliage reads full without bloating the mesh, and placing one leafy twig near the koala's mouth for a natural touch.

I'm deciding against cluttering the koala's face with extra sprigs, keeping nothing directly in front of it. For the base, I'm building an octagonal lathe stand with two stepped tiers, a chamfer, and wood paint, considering stubby feet and a small front plaque—maybe with an engraved leaf emblem instead of pixel text since lettering would be tricky to render cleanly.

Adding rope wraps as lathe rings at the trunk-seat junction, then sketching the seat branch as a swept path from trunk to front with a tapering radius and a flat end cap for a clean finish.

Now I'm working out the vertical geometry: computing the seat top height from the branch radius, then aligning the rump bottom and hip cap dimensions so the rounded hip dome meets the seat surface correctly.

I'm also plotting the toe arcs and foot pad positions, then checking the leg segment lengths from hip to knee to ankle to make sure the shin isn't too short, adjusting the knee and ankle coordinates to get proportions that look right for a koala.

Still working out coordinates...

I should check the shoulder-to-wrist distance stays under reach limits with these arm lengths, but I'm worried the current branch position makes the koala look like it's reaching backward awkwardly from the camera view. I'll shift the trunk forward and curve the branches toward the front so the arms read as hugging naturally, while leaning the torso forward too.

I'm tuning the trunk and hip positions so the body silhouette just touches the branch without overlapping badly, then adjusting the V-branch grip points to match the paw height. Deciding to skip extra hanging ornaments and move on to defining the main trunk path coordinates.

For the trunk, I'm sketching how it curves upward, forks into the V-branches around y≈0.7, then continues as a central leader up to a canopy top — but realizing 1.9 feels too tall against the koala's position, so I'm scaling the leader and V-branch tips down to around y=1.65 for better proportion.

Now I need to attach twigs at the branch tips, so I'm designing a helper function that builds a small rod sweeping outward with droop and returns leaf attachment frames along its length, alternating sides. The tricky part is leaf-to-bone assignment — if I let leaves snap to the nearest skeletal joint automatically, they might wrongly attach to the koala's arm or hand bones instead of the tree, so I need to explicitly pass the correct bone reference to avoid that mix-up.

I'm deciding to make the hips the root joint for the stand structure, and passing an explicit bone reference to all stand-related rods and parts so nothing accidentally rigs to the koala itself. Now I'm settling on texture scale (0.02 per fur cell, half that for fine pixel details) and sketching out a small pixel-art leaf shape with outline, body, highlight, and midtone colors.

Sketching leaf pixel rows...

Still designing the pixel grid...

Now I'm thinking about bark strip coloring with lighter cream or dark tan tones, adding small gum nut clusters near leaf nodes, and planning fur shading details using cell-paint ramps to give the koala more depth.

I want cream cheek tufts, ear tufts, a chest bib, a textured nose highlight, pale claws, and darker brow shading boxes above the eyes for definition. I'm also considering adding scattered fur tuft cards across the torso and arms using a small pixel texture to break up the silhouette with fuzzy edges.

Working through the scatter approach, I'm planning around 90 tufts across the body plus denser coverage on the rump, using a mix of light and dark pixel tuft textures without extra tinting, and thinking through how the card orientation and flow direction should lean so the tufts read correctly when viewed from the front.

I'll turn on cross geometry for the tufts to keep them visible from more angles, which stays cheap enough at this tuft count, then move on to designing ear fluff planes and crown tufts before sketching out the eye textures with a small pixel grid for the bead and highlight.

Now I'm designing the nose texture, a small pixel grid giving the nose box a dark body color with a lighter highlight patch and darker nostril slits, meant to be applied to the front face of the nose box.

I'm realizing the textured box would apply the drawing to all faces, so instead I'll keep the nose box a plain dark color and overlay the detailed texture as a separate decal plane on the front. I'm also sketching a simple thin line decal for the mouth to sit below the nose on the muzzle.

Now I'm working out the head's local coordinate system, placing the cranium block relative to the head center so I can position each facial feature consistently.

Continuing to define offsets for the crown, cheeks, muzzle, and nose, each as sized boxes positioned relative to the cranium's front and vertical extents to build the face profile in depth.

The nose sits atop the muzzle, positioned to clear the eyes horizontally; I'm also planning a lighter cream-colored paint around the muzzle for the mask effect, and placing the lower jaw box just beneath the muzzle to form the jaw joint.

For the mouth, I'm adding a dark interior slab on top of the jaw to suggest depth, with the muzzle bottom and jaw top aligned so there's no visible gap between them.

For the ears, I'm positioning them at the top sides of the cranium as circular outlines extruded forward along the z-axis, so they face the viewer like the rest of the face.

Placing ear centers out past the cranium radius so they stick out visibly, checking the depth so they sit slightly behind the face front. Now working on the inner ear texture plane positioned just in front of the ear surface, sized to fit within the ear circle.

Writing ear texture pixels...

I need to position the ear's center by offsetting from the origin point using the direction vectors so it sits correctly on the head. Then for the cheek fluff tufts, I'm planning small stepped triangular outlines, narrow at bottom widening upward to form a downward-pointing tuft, placed along the outward-facing side of the cheeks.

Setting up the extrusion axes so the tuft plane faces sideways with thickness along the x-axis, placing three tufts per cheek at different depth offsets with varying heights for a natural look. I'm skipping chin fur for now and moving on to writing a generic fur-paint function that varies tone based on body position.

For the coloring, I'm picking a gray-blue koala palette with a lighter belly ramp, and defining a cell-paint function that blends normal direction and random noise to produce natural-looking fur variation.

Now I'm painting the body by detecting the chest/belly region through a rough elliptical mask in the front-facing area, adding jagged noise to the edge, and blending in a cream-colored ramp there while keeping the rump gray.

For the head, I'm layering fur with lighter cheeks and a cream-gray muzzle, then adding dark pads for the hands and a vertical streaked bark texture for the branch.

For the main body fur, I'm setting a base color ramp from tan to cream, then adding salmon-pink patches on higher noise values, olive-grey patches on lower ones, and a darker rough zone near the bottom with random dark specks, plus a darker stocking effect at the trunk base.

Twigs get a flat reddish-brown tone, and I'm planning a brass plaque emblem with a leaf motif using pixel art, positioned on the base's front flat face, figuring out the octagon lathe geometry to place it correctly.

Settling on a 0.18x0.05 plaque sized to a small pixel texture, and sketching a simple pixel pattern for a leaf emblem with dark borders and a fill color.

Still mapping out the pixel grid...

I'm now adding the finishing details: a rope lashing around the support post and branch junction, plus working out the dimensions and placement of a prop post connecting the base to the seat branch.

I'm skipping extra flourishes like mushrooms or lichen and tallying up the overall part count — trunk, branches, seat, base, post, ropes, koala body, head, ears, eyes, arms, and digits — to keep the build manageable.

Now I'm setting up the actual build script, importing the builder, frame, math, path, and IK utilities from the SDK, then starting to define the joint hierarchy with the hips as the root and building out the spine chain.

Working out the head-torso overlap so the neck tucks under the chunky head, then sketching a radius profile along the body sweep for a pot-bellied torso shape tapering toward the tail end.

Now I'm setting up the arm shoulder points, checking they sit flush against the body surface so the arm roots appear buried rather than floating outside, and starting to chain the shoulder joint to the spine's chest joint.

Defining radius values for the arm taper, then working out the hand geometry—a palm box oriented so it presses flat against the bar with fingers wrapping around, figuring out the basis vectors for orientation.

I'll use `dir: D, up: u` as the parameter names for aiming the part, confirming the cheat sheet's naming convention. The hand's tip joint anchors to the palm bone, and I'm now working out the wrist target position by placing the palm center offset from the branch axis by its thickness.

For the fingers, I'm laying out digit paths as arcs around the branch axis - radius just slightly larger than the branch so they hug it, with fingers sweeping one direction and thumbs sweeping the opposite direction so they oppose each other in grip.

I'm now spacing the three fingers and two thumbs along the branch axis, giving each digit its own offset so they distribute naturally across a palm roughly 0.14 units long, with the palm center shifted slightly to balance them.

For the branch I'm tapering the radius linearly from 0.06 down to 0.028, keeping the octagonal cross-section consistent. I'm also picking a rotation sign for the finger curl direction by comparing which orientation gives a higher world-y position at the arc midpoint, so fingers curl upward and thumbs curl the opposite way.

Now I'm laying out the finger joint path as a few angle steps smoothed with a catmull curve, tapering the sweep radius toward the tip, and starting the claw spike as a continuation from the fingertip along its tangent direction.

I'm extending the claw spike with its own length, radius, and bone color tied to the chain's last joint, then moving on to set up the feet similarly—defining the ankle grip axis and seat position, mirroring the hand's gripping-finger helper but rotated around the foot's side vector instead.

Now I'm tapering the seat radius from trunk to tip, placing the sole pad box using the same dimension logic as the palm, and tracing the ankle's position back through the leg chain from the knee down.

Checking shin length against the knee-to-ankle distance, then verifying thigh length from hip to knee — both come out close to target values, confirming the joint placements. Now I'm naming the leg chain joints (hip, knee, ankle) for each side.

Working out the thigh taper radii from hip to knee, then moving to the foot — placing five toes spread along the z-axis, with the big toe positioned opposite the others and non-clawed.

Checking the toe arcs where they wrap over the top of the branch, I realize the left and right feet's toe positions could collide at identical z-coordinates, causing overlapping geometry where both feet meet at the top — I need to offset one foot's z slightly to avoid the z-fighting.

The sign choice works automatically based on mean y position, so the toes curl correctly over the top for both feet with tips spanning 15 to 115 degrees. Now I'm working out the branch point geometry using the path's position and tangent at parameter tg, and checking shoulder reach distances against the branch control points.

Checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance, about 0.25, fits within arm segment lengths of 0.17 each for a believable elbow bend outward and down. I need to make sure the raised hands at that height don't collide with the head's width and ear span.

The hand sits clear below the ear, but checking the arm path from shoulder to wrist, it looks like the forearm might clip through the head's cheek area near the overlapping x/z ranges. That's a minor collision I should fix by adjusting the shoulder position outward.

Moving the shoulder lower and farther out, with the grip point pushed further out too, keeps the arm trajectory clear of the cheek boundary by a small margin. Now I need to work out the torso radius at shoulder height to confirm the shoulder sits right on the surface, then move on to defining arm radius and the leaf twig structure.

I'm building a twig path that droops downward using a curve through root, midpoint, and tip, with a tapered rod shape and bone-colored material. Along this path I'm placing leaves at intervals, alternating their direction to either side and biasing them to hang downward based on blending the tangent with a lateral and downward vector, then orienting each leaf card to that frame.

Now I'm checking the leaf card details — making sure the root sits at the frame origin with the tip pointing away, orienting the face normal along the flattened flow axis so it's visible from both sides, and varying the spin randomly. I'm also considering adding a slight bend to curl the tips toward the viewer for a softer look, though I need to watch out for back-facing issues.

Next I'm planning twig placement: distributing texture variants between pointed leaves and rounder juvenile leaves near the top, then working out how each branch spawns several twigs along its length plus a tip twig, with twig root direction computed by blending the branch tangent with an alternating sideways offset.

I'm sizing out twig lengths and leaf card dimensions, checking that the aspect ratio stays close to square-pixel accuracy for the leaf sprites, and tallying up roughly 126 total leaf cards across all branches and twigs.

Now I'm adding small gum nuts as low-poly spheres with brown bodies and dark caps scattered along twigs, plus setting up bark strip scattering across the trunk surface with distance and height filtering so the strips don't cluster unnaturally.

For the bark strips I'm using flat earthy colors (tan, khaki, brown tones) randomly assigned, keeping the total unique flat color count under the 64-material limit, and starting to define the trunk's curved path using a catmull-rom spline through a series of control points.

Writing trunk parameters...

Working through matching the octagon's flat-face orientation to the circle segments, I realize I need to rotate the end cap by 22.5° to align vertices properly, but since orientation priority favors dir over rotation, I'll need to bake the rotation into the geometry itself instead.

I'm checking the seat and hips measurements for vertical alignment, confirming the top surface height, hip start position, and foot grip center all line up with the path values, then moving to the base stand lathe design using flat tiers similar to prior helper geometry.

Still writing base geometry...

Adding 4 fallen leaves plus 2 pebbles, then checking that the trunk and post positions sit within the base's flat radius, that bounding extents stay centered, and that the model's lowest point touches the floor. I'm also sketching wood grain paint logic for the base top using concentric rings based on radial distance.

For the head, I'm defining eye placement using a helper function offset from the cranium center, then adding a darker eye-patch decal just behind each eye with a small z-gap to avoid z-fighting flicker.

Adding nose and mouth decals now too: the nose as a small plane near the muzzle front with a modest texture resolution, and the mouth as a thin line plane positioned just below it on the jaw.

I'm also planning color details — tinting the muzzle box a cream-grey, the nose a near-black shade, and the cheeks slightly lighter — while leaving eyebrows out for now and considering adding a few small tuft cards scattered on the head and ears for extra fur texture.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton: head and jaw parts assigned to their respective bones, with the jaw joint parented to the head and aimed forward, ear joints acting as hinges angled outward, and the head joint parenting from the last spine joint in the neck chain with its direction oriented upward and forward.

I'm computing the chest cream patch coloring in world coordinates and scattering small tuft cards across the body surface using a filtered sweep, with a pixel-art texture for each tuft.

Writing pixel art pattern...

I'm also setting up grey and cream palettes for the tufts, splitting them based on whether they land on the cream chest region or elsewhere on the body.

I'm sizing the fur cards small and deciding not to bother with extra fringe on the arms or wrists, keeping the rig simple with hips and a four-joint spine.

Working out the joint count: head, jaw, two ears, one stand, six arm joints, six leg joints, and forty digit joints for a total of 63. I'm naming digit chains per limb and parenting them to the arm/leg tip joints, then writing a helper that wraps points around a surface for building each digit's path.

Still writing path generator...

I'll sweep the chain into a 6-sided tapered tube with rounded caps for the finger shape, using catmull-rom interpolation through the joint points. For coloring, I'm going with a dark leathery gray for the hand and pads, a darker fur tone for the fingers, and a bone-like tan for the claws.

Before finalizing the limb direction, I should check the ik module's import signature and the builder's exported helpers like stick and decal, plus the frame export.

input.command: cat src/ik.ts | head -60; grep -n "export" src/frame.ts | head -20; grep -n "export" src/builder.ts | head -30; grep -n "tangentAt\|closestT" src/path.ts | head
